Elastane.deeper: The US rule defines spandex as a manufactured fiber of at least 85 percent segmented polyurethane. Long, flexible soft segments, typically polyether or polyester glycols, alternate with short hard segments built from an aromatic diisocyanate chain-extended with diols or diamines. The hard segments aggregate into hydrogen-bonded domains that act as physical cross-links, while the soft segments coil above their glass transition, so stretching uncoils them and the domains pull the network back. Spandex is generally dry spun from polar solvents such as dimethylacetamide into coalesced multifilaments. Small amounts create a large recycling problem: elastane content in blends generally ranges from 1 to 20 percent, and one study notes that even small amounts can block fiber-to-fiber recycling of cotton. Aminolysis in dimethyl sulfoxide with diethylenetriamine at 80 C for 2 hours reduced residual elastane below 0.08 percent in recovered cellulose.
Elastane.origins: Elastane was developed in the mid-twentieth century as a lighter, more durable alternative to rubber thread, and LYCRA, which grew out of DuPont's fiber business, became a widely recognized brand. Because the fiber arrived as a manufactured class, it received regulated generic names under labeling law: spandex in the United States, under the Federal Trade Commission's list in 16 CFR 303.7, and elastane in the European Union, under Annex I to Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011. The two words describe the same polymer class.

Filament.deeper: Silk is the natural reference point. A Bombyx mori cocoon is wound from one continuous filament; the FAO reports total lengths of about 600 to 1,500 m, of which about 80 percent is typically reelable, and individual cocoon filaments average only about 1.5 to 3.5 denier, so raw silk combines filaments from roughly 2 to 20 cocoons. Manufactured filaments are extruded through spinneret holes and drawn, which aligns chains and raises tenacity; partially oriented yarn can then be draw-textured, a route one review says handles about 60 percent of melt-spun filament yarn. Because filaments run the full length of the yarn, multifilament yarns need little or no twist to hold together, whereas staple yarns rely on twist-generated friction. Filament tow can also be cut into staple, so a polymer name alone never tells you which form a yarn uses.
Filament.origins: The word is built on the Latin filum, thread. For most of history silk was the only natural textile filament used at scale. The first manufactured filaments came from cellulose solutions: in 1890 Louis-Henri Despeissis patented spinning fibers from cuprammonium cellulose solutions, and by 1891 Max Fremery and Johann Urban were making lamp filaments by this route at Oberbruch near Aachen. Melt spinning followed in the twentieth century with nylon at DuPont, where Wallace Carothers' group developed polyamides that could be drawn into strong filaments.

Finishing.deeper: Finishes work by mechanical, thermal or chemical means: raising, compacting and fulling rearrange fibers; heat setting relaxes and locks thermoplastic structure above its glass transition; mercerization swells cotton in roughly 20 to 26 percent sodium hydroxide; repellent finishes change surface energy. Durable water repellents show why a finish needs chemistry and testing, not just a name. After long-chain PFAS were phased out, alternatives fell into four groups: side-chain fluorinated polymers, silicones, hydrocarbons and other chemistries such as dendrimers and inorganic nanoparticles, and the non-fluorinated options lack oil repellence. Side-chain fluorinated polymers are barely extractable, so one study found extraction-based analysis captured roughly 25 to 50 times less fluorine than oxidation or hydrolysis methods. Durability is tested after laundering: one fluorine-free silica and silicone finish, applied by pad-dry-cure, kept top spray ratings after five standard wash cycles.
Finishing.origins: Finishing is as old as cloth making. Roman fullers cleaned and finished wool cloth with urine and absorbent clays, and the clay called fuller's earth is named for that work. Chemical finishing entered the industrial era with John Mercer, a Lancashire calico printer who observed the action of caustic soda on cotton in 1844 and patented the treatment in 1850; Horace A. Lowe patented treatment under tension, which produces luster, in 1889. Heat setting became essential with melt-spun synthetic fibers in the mid-twentieth century.

Ginning.deeper: Two mechanisms dominate. In a saw gin, rotating toothed saws catch the lint and draw it through gaps between ribs that are too narrow for the seed to pass, after which the fibers are removed from the teeth. In a roller gin, lint clings to a moving roller and is pulled past a close-fitting knife while a rotating bar or knife strips the seed away. Roller ginning is the gentler process: it leaves fewer fiber entanglements (neps) and preserves the length of extra-long-staple cottons such as Pima, whose fine fibers saw teeth tend to break and tangle. Saw gins descend from machines designed for short-staple upland cotton. Recent economic work in the United States compares the relative cost of ginning with saw, conventional roller and high-speed roller gins, so the choice of gin is both a fiber-quality and a cost decision.
Ginning.origins: Gin is a shortening of 'engine'. Eli Whitney applied for a patent on his cotton gin on October 28, 1793, and it was granted on March 14, 1794; the National Archives holds the patent drawing. His machine used a toothed wheel to pull fibers through a fine metal mesh, leaving the seeds behind, and was designed for short-staple cotton; a single device could clean up to about fifty pounds of cotton a day. The expansion of cotton growing that followed created a vast new market for enslaved labor in the United States.

Greasy wool.deeper: The non-fiber fraction of a raw fleece has three main parts. Wool grease, the source of lanolin, is water-insoluble and is dominated by esters: studies describe lanolin as a source of branched-chain sterol esters and wax esters, and one analysis of scouring-effluent grease identified sterol esters as its most important components. Suint, the dried sweat, is water-soluble and rich in potassium salts; reported wool-scouring effluents contain roughly 4,200 to 13,000 mg of potassium per liter. Dirt, dust and vegetable matter make up the rest. Because the clean-fiber share varies from fleece to fleece, sale lots are sampled by coring the bales, and IWTO-28 applies the airflow method to raw-wool core samples so that mean fiber diameter can be certified before scouring. Wool grease is removed industrially by emulsifying it with detergent, which is why scouring effluent is high in chemical oxygen demand.
Greasy wool.origins: Fine wool is still traded in three forms that mark successive stages: greasy fleece, scoured wool and combed top. Certification of greasy lots matured in the late twentieth century: IWTO accepted test method IWTO-28 in 1971, allowing mean diameter of sale lots to be certified from core samples, and in 1995 accepted the Laserscan and OFDA methods for raw wool and top. The grease itself became a commodity as lanolin, and dermatologists have recognized allergy to lanolin and its derivatives for decades.
